quests.hint: 'More often than not' is inserted right after the subject, meaning 'usually'.
quests.explanation: 'More often than not' is an idiomatic way of saying 'usually', slightly more elegant than the plain word. This sentence redefines courage in a way that feels both simple and genuinely true.
quests.textToSpeak: Courage, more often than not, has very little to do with feeling unafraid and almost everything to do with acting well despite the fear.
quests.correctAnswer: Courage, more often than not, has very little to do with feeling unafraid and almost everything to do with acting well despite the fear.

quests.hint: 'So rarely does courage announce itself' inverts 'does' and 'courage' after 'so rarely'.
quests.explanation: 'Announce itself' personifies courage as something that could loudly introduce its own presence, which this sentence argues it rarely does. 'From the inside' contrasts how something appears with how it's actually experienced.
quests.textToSpeak: So rarely does courage announce itself with confidence that most brave decisions, from the inside, feel a great deal more like quiet terror.
quests.correctAnswer: So rarely does courage announce itself with confidence that most brave decisions, from the inside, feel a great deal more like quiet terror.

quests.hint: 'Seen closely enough' is inserted mid-sentence, meaning 'when examined carefully'.
quests.explanation: This cleft sentence, beginning with 'What', gently redefines a grand word, bravery, in humble, human terms. 'Every reasonable urge to stop' acknowledges that hesitation is entirely normal, not a failure.
quests.textToSpeak: What we call bravery, seen closely enough, usually turns out to be an ordinary person continuing to move forward despite every reasonable urge to stop.
quests.correctAnswer: What we call bravery, seen closely enough, usually turns out to be an ordinary person continuing to move forward despite every reasonable urge to stop.

quests.hint: 'If only because' introduces a reason, even a minor one, worth mentioning.
quests.explanation: 'If only because' introduces a single reason among possibly several, often the simplest or clearest one. 'Performing sincerity' is a pointed phrase capturing a genuinely modern paradox about self-presentation.
quests.textToSpeak: Authenticity is harder to define than most people assume, if only because performing sincerity has become almost as easy as feeling it genuinely.
quests.correctAnswer: Authenticity is harder to define than most people assume, if only because performing sincerity has become almost as easy as feeling it genuinely.

quests.hint: 'Rarely is anyone' inverts 'is' and 'anyone' after 'rarely'.
quests.explanation: The semicolon contrasts a common oversimplification with a more accurate, nuanced view of personality. 'Whichever part happens to be convenient' suggests identity is partly shaped by circumstance, not fixed.
quests.textToSpeak: Rarely is anyone entirely one thing; most people are simply better, in any given moment, at showing whichever part happens to be convenient.
quests.correctAnswer: Rarely is anyone entirely one thing; most people are simply better, in any given moment, at showing whichever part happens to be convenient.

quests.hint: 'Passes for' means 'is mistakenly accepted as', not simply 'is'.
quests.explanation: 'Pass for something' means to be accepted as that thing, even if the label isn't fully accurate. This sentence makes a sharp, self-aware point about the paradox of appearing effortlessly genuine.
quests.textToSpeak: So much of what passes for authenticity online is, on reflection, simply a more polished performance of appearing not to be performing at all.
quests.correctAnswer: So much of what passes for authenticity online is, on reflection, simply a more polished performance of appearing not to be performing at all.

quests.hint: 'Along the way' means during the process, not just at the final destination.
quests.explanation: 'Along the way' figuratively describes the ongoing process of a life or journey, not just its final outcome. This sentence offers a quietly moving redefinition of a big, often intimidating word: legacy.
quests.textToSpeak: Legacy rarely turns out to be the grand achievement someone hoped for; more often, it's simply how they treated people along the way.
quests.correctAnswer: Legacy rarely turns out to be the grand achievement someone hoped for; more often, it's simply how they treated people along the way.

quests.hint: 'Few people... most' sets up a clear, memorable contrast between two groups.
quests.explanation: 'Few... most' contrasts a smaller, unusual group with the larger, more typical one. 'While achieving it' shows the two things, achievement and kindness, happening together, not as separate choices.
quests.textToSpeak: Few people are remembered, in the end, for what they achieved alone; most are remembered for how they made other people feel while achieving it.
quests.correctAnswer: Few people are remembered, in the end, for what they achieved alone; most are remembered for how they made other people feel while achieving it.

quests.hint: 'Generation after generation' repeats the noun for emphasis, meaning across a very long time.
quests.explanation: Repeating a noun with 'after' between, as in 'generation after generation', emphasises continuity across a long stretch of time. 'A handful of' means a small number, useful for describing something valuable but limited.
quests.textToSpeak: What ultimately gets carried forward, generation after generation, tends to be a handful of stories and a particular way of making someone feel welcome.
quests.correctAnswer: What ultimately gets carried forward, generation after generation, tends to be a handful of stories and a particular way of making someone feel welcome.

quests.hint: 'So often does language fail us' inverts 'does' and 'language' after 'so often'.
quests.explanation: 'Fail us' personifies language as something that can let a person down, precisely when it's needed most. 'What was left unsaid' turns an absence, silence, into the actual subject of the sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: So often does language fail us in exactly the moments that matter most that entire relationships have been quietly shaped by what was left unsaid.
quests.correctAnswer: So often does language fail us in exactly the moments that matter most that entire relationships have been quietly shaped by what was left unsaid.

quests.hint: 'Spoken at precisely the right moment' is inserted right after the subject for emphasis.
quests.explanation: This sentence compares a single small action to an entire year, a deliberately extreme contrast for emphasis. 'Well-meaning silence' pairs a positive intention with a passive, ultimately unhelpful outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: The right word, spoken at precisely the right moment, can do more for another person than an entire year of otherwise well-meaning silence.
quests.correctAnswer: The right word, spoken at precisely the right moment, can do more for another person than an entire year of otherwise well-meaning silence.

quests.hint: 'Learning to say a difficult thing kindly' as a subject pairs with the singular verb 'may be'.
quests.explanation: 'Rather than X or Y' rules out two common alternatives before naming the better option. 'Underrated' means valued less than it deserves, a precise and useful word for describing overlooked skills.
quests.textToSpeak: Learning to say a difficult thing kindly, rather than avoiding it or saying it carelessly, may be one of the most underrated skills anyone can develop.
quests.correctAnswer: Learning to say a difficult thing kindly, rather than avoiding it or saying it carelessly, may be one of the most underrated skills anyone can develop.

quests.hint: 'So gradually that' links a description of pace to its surprising result.
quests.explanation: 'So + adverb + that' is the familiar pattern seen throughout this level, describing an extreme degree leading to a result. 'Who they used to be' reuses the earlier structure 'used to' for describing a past identity.
quests.textToSpeak: Change tends to arrive so gradually that most people only recognise it in hindsight, looking back at who they used to be.
quests.correctAnswer: Change tends to arrive so gradually that most people only recognise it in hindsight, looking back at who they used to be.

quests.hint: 'So slowly does a person typically change' inverts 'does' and 'a person' after 'so slowly'.
quests.explanation: This sentence contrasts two perspectives, daily closeness and long absence, to make a vivid point about how change is actually perceived. 'At once' here means immediately, all in a single moment.
quests.textToSpeak: So slowly does a person typically change that daily company notices almost nothing, while an old friend, absent for years, notices everything at once.
quests.correctAnswer: So slowly does a person typically change that daily company notices almost nothing, while an old friend, absent for years, notices everything at once.

quests.hint: 'From the inside' and 'to a distant observer' offer two contrasting viewpoints.
quests.explanation: This cleft sentence contrasts internal experience with external perspective, two viewpoints that can genuinely disagree about the same situation. 'In the middle of becoming' emphasises an ongoing, unfinished process.
quests.textToSpeak: What feels, from the inside, like standing still is very often, to a distant observer, someone in the middle of becoming someone else.
quests.correctAnswer: What feels, from the inside, like standing still is very often, to a distant observer, someone in the middle of becoming someone else.

quests.hint: 'Sustained long enough and aimed in roughly the right direction' is inserted right after the subject.
quests.explanation: 'Outperform' means to do better than something else, precise vocabulary for a comparison of results. 'Than talent would like to admit' playfully personifies talent as having pride, a light touch of humour in a thoughtful sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Curiosity, sustained long enough and aimed in roughly the right direction, tends to outperform raw talent more often than talent would like to admit.
quests.correctAnswer: Curiosity, sustained long enough and aimed in roughly the right direction, tends to outperform raw talent more often than talent would like to admit.

quests.hint: 'So easily is real curiosity mistaken' inverts 'is' and 'real curiosity' after 'so easily'.
quests.explanation: 'Mere' before a noun suggests something is being unfairly dismissed as trivial. This sentence uses irony: the very trait behind someone's ability gets mistaken for a flaw and then suppressed.
quests.textToSpeak: So easily is real curiosity mistaken for mere distraction that capable people sometimes learn to quietly suppress the very trait that made them capable.
quests.correctAnswer: So easily is real curiosity mistaken for mere distraction that capable people sometimes learn to quietly suppress the very trait that made them capable.

quests.hint: The semicolon separates a rejected explanation from the one the sentence actually supports.
quests.explanation: This sentence uses a cleft structure plus a semicolon to first rule out an expected explanation (discipline) before offering a warmer, more human one (curiosity). 'Worth asking' is a compact way of saying 'that deserved to be asked'.
quests.textToSpeak: What made you interesting as a child was rarely discipline; it was almost certainly a willingness to ask questions nobody else thought worth asking.
quests.correctAnswer: What made you interesting as a child was rarely discipline; it was almost certainly a willingness to ask questions nobody else thought worth asking.

quests.hint: 'Arrive sideways' is a metaphor meaning to come indirectly, almost by accident.
quests.explanation: 'Arrive sideways' is a vivid, spatial metaphor for something reached indirectly rather than head-on. 'For its own sake' means for no other reason than the activity itself, a subtle but important distinction.
quests.textToSpeak: Meaning tends to arrive sideways, through work done carefully for its own sake, rather than through the direct and often exhausting pursuit of meaning itself.
quests.correctAnswer: Meaning tends to arrive sideways, through work done carefully for its own sake, rather than through the direct and often exhausting pursuit of meaning itself.

quests.hint: 'So directly does the pursuit... seem' inverts 'does' and 'the pursuit' after 'so directly'.
quests.explanation: 'Undermine itself' describes something working against its own goal, a genuinely paradoxical and thought-provoking idea. 'Contented' is a calm, settled alternative to the more intense word 'happy'.
quests.textToSpeak: So directly does the pursuit of happiness seem to undermine itself that many of the most contented people report barely thinking about happiness at all.
quests.correctAnswer: So directly does the pursuit of happiness seem to undermine itself that many of the most contented people report barely thinking about happiness at all.

quests.hint: 'From a distance' and 'up close' offer two contrasting levels of detail.
quests.explanation: This cleft sentence again contrasts a distant, simplified view with a closer, more detailed one. 'Dozens of smaller, quieter choices' offers a grounded, encouraging alternative to the idea of one grand, defining passion.
quests.textToSpeak: What looks, from a distance, like a life built around one passion is, up close, almost always built from dozens of smaller, quieter choices.
quests.correctAnswer: What looks, from a distance, like a life built around one passion is, up close, almost always built from dozens of smaller, quieter choices.

quests.hint: 'Especially on the harder days' is inserted mid-sentence, adding warmth and empathy.
quests.explanation: 'It's worth remembering that' reintroduces a comforting fact at a moment it's likely to be needed. 'Especially on the harder days' inserted mid-sentence adds a warm, personal, encouraging tone.
quests.textToSpeak: It's worth remembering, especially on the harder days, that almost everyone you admire has, at some point, seriously considered giving up entirely.
quests.correctAnswer: It's worth remembering, especially on the harder days, that almost everyone you admire has, at some point, seriously considered giving up entirely.

quests.hint: 'So universal is the experience' inverts 'is' and 'the experience' after 'so universal'.
quests.explanation: This sentence playfully reverses expectation: instead of doubt being the worrying thing, its complete absence is presented as the stranger, more concerning case. 'Near total absence' means almost, but not quite, completely missing.
quests.textToSpeak: So universal is the experience of self-doubt that its near total absence, when you actually encounter it, should probably worry you more than reassure you.
quests.correctAnswer: So universal is the experience of self-doubt that its near total absence, when you actually encounter it, should probably worry you more than reassure you.

quests.hint: 'What separates X from Y' works as the subject of the whole sentence.
quests.explanation: This cleft sentence again rules out an expected explanation, talent, in favour of a more human one: persistence. 'The hundredth disappointment' is a deliberately specific, vivid number rather than a vague 'many'.
quests.textToSpeak: What separates those who eventually succeed from those who quietly give up is rarely talent; it's simply a refusal to stop after the hundredth disappointment.
quests.correctAnswer: What separates those who eventually succeed from those who quietly give up is rarely talent; it's simply a refusal to stop after the hundredth disappointment.

quests.hint: 'Resist translation' personifies ideas as actively pushing back against being translated.
quests.explanation: 'Resist' applied to ideas personifies them as capable of pushing back, adding vividness to an abstract linguistic point. 'Never needed a single word for' explains untranslatability through necessity rather than difficulty.
quests.textToSpeak: Every language carries ideas that resist translation, small untranslatable feelings that speakers of other languages have simply never needed a single word for.
quests.correctAnswer: Every language carries ideas that resist translation, small untranslatable feelings that speakers of other languages have simply never needed a single word for.

quests.hint: 'Lost and gained... at once' balances two opposite outcomes happening together.
quests.explanation: 'Lost and gained... at once' balances two seemingly contradictory outcomes as simultaneously true, a nuanced view of translation. 'Care less about X than about Y' shows a considered set of priorities.
quests.textToSpeak: So much is lost and gained in translation at once that the best translators care less about exact words than about preserving the original feeling.
quests.correctAnswer: So much is lost and gained in translation at once that the best translators care less about exact words than about preserving the original feeling.

quests.hint: This list of three factors — speaker, listener, and the unsaid — closes with the least expected one.
quests.explanation: Listing three factors, with the final one being the most surprising, 'everything left unsaid', is a satisfying rhetorical technique. This cleft sentence makes a thoughtful final point about the nature of meaning itself.
quests.textToSpeak: What a word ultimately means always depends a little on who is speaking it, who is listening, and everything left unsaid between them.
quests.correctAnswer: What a word ultimately means always depends a little on who is speaking it, who is listening, and everything left unsaid between them.

quests.hint: 'Repeating every sentence in this course aloud' is inserted mid-sentence, describing the listener's own effort.
quests.explanation: This sentence speaks directly to the learner completing this very course, a warm, personal way to close a long journey. 'More than you've noticed' reassures that growth often happens gradually, beneath conscious awareness.
quests.textToSpeak: If you've made it this far, repeating every sentence in this course aloud, your spoken English has almost certainly grown more than you've noticed.
quests.correctAnswer: If you've made it this far, repeating every sentence in this course aloud, your spoken English has almost certainly grown more than you've noticed.

quests.hint: The semicolon contrasts a common misconception about fluency with a truer definition.
quests.explanation: This sentence redefines 'fluency' itself, moving away from the idea of a fixed finish line towards an ongoing, comfortable relationship with speaking. 'Whatever you actually mean to say' emphasises genuine self-expression over perfection.
quests.textToSpeak: Fluency was never really about reaching some final, finished level; it was always about becoming steadily more comfortable saying whatever you actually mean to say.
quests.correctAnswer: Fluency was never really about reaching some final, finished level; it was always about becoming steadily more comfortable saying whatever you actually mean to say.

quests.hint: 'Not X, but Y' contrasts a common misconception with a warmer, truer conclusion.
quests.explanation: This final sentence uses 'not X, but Y' to reframe the entire idea of finishing a language course. Fittingly, it ends this journey the same way it began: with the simple, ongoing act of speaking.
quests.textToSpeak: It turns out the real finish line was never a fixed level of perfection, but simply the quiet, ongoing confidence to keep on speaking.
quests.correctAnswer: It turns out the real finish line was never a fixed level of perfection, but simply the quiet, ongoing confidence to keep on speaking.
